'''Cock-a-leekie soup''' is a [[Scottish cuisine|Scottish]] [[soup]] dish consisting of [[leek]]s and [[Black pepper|pepper]]ed [[chicken stock]], often thickened with [[rice]], or sometimes [[barley]]. The original recipe added [[prune]]s during cooking, and traditionalists still garnish with a [[julienning|julienne]] of prunes.

While it is called "Scotland's National Soup",<ref>{{cite book |last=Whitman |first=Joan |title=Craig Claiborne’s The New York Times Food Encyclopedia |location=New York |publisher=The New York Times Company |date=1985}}</ref> it probably originated as a chicken and onion soup in [[France]].{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}} By the late 16th century,<ref>{{cite web|website= The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2017/nov/23/how-to-make-the-perfect-cock-a-leekie-soup|title=How to make the perfect cock-a-leekie soup}} Retrieved October 17, 2019</ref> it had made its way to Scotland, where the onions were replaced with leeks.<ref name="AytoJohn">Ayto, John. An A to Z of Food & Drink, John Ayto. Oxford:Oxford University Press, 2002</ref> The first recipe was printed in 1598,<ref name="AytoJohn" /> though the name "cock-a-leekie" did not come into use until the 18th century.<ref>Davidson, Alan. Oxford Companion to Food, Alan Davidson. Oxford:Oxford University Press, 1999</ref>
